title: Plant Growth and Development
tagline: Meristems, the phases of growth, and the hormones that decide what a plant becomes.

overview.intro: This chapter explains how a plant grows — where growth happens, how it is measured and what its phases are — and then how growth is directed, by the five classes of plant hormone and by the environmental signals that switch development between vegetative and flowering. The examination pattern is predictable: define a term with its condition, describe an experiment such as the photoperiodism or auxin curvature test, compare two hormones in a table, or explain how a hormone produces its effect at the cellular level.

facts.label: Sites of growth
facts.value: Meristems: apical at shoot and root tips, lateral in the cambium, and intercalary at the base of grass leaves and nodes.

facts.label: Phases
facts.value: Meristematic or cell division phase, elongation phase, and maturation or differentiation phase.

facts.label: Five hormones
facts.value: Auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid and ethylene — two promoting, one inhibiting, one gaseous.

facts.label: Photoperiodism
facts.value: The response of flowering to day length, mediated by phytochrome, with short-day, long-day and day-neutral plants.

learningOutcomes: Define growth and its three phases, and locate the meristems.
Describe the functions of each class of plant hormone with examples.
Explain the mechanism of auxin action at the cellular level.
State the differentials of growth and use them in simple calculations.
Explain photoperiodism and the role of phytochrome in flowering.

learn.title: Growth, meristems and the phases of development

blocks.text: Growth is a permanent and irreversible increase in size or dry mass, and in plants it is largely irreversible because a cell that has differentiated does not return to being a meristematic one. It can be measured as absolute increase in length or mass, as absolute growth rate relative to the initial value, or as relative growth rate, which is the increase per unit of initial quantity and is what allows a small seedling and a large plant to be compared. At the cellular level growth has three phases. The meristematic phase is the region of active cell division, where cells are small, thin-walled, dense in cytoplasm with large nuclei and no large vacuoles, and divide rapidly. The phase of elongation follows, where the cells enlarge mainly by taking up water into a growing vacuole, stretching the wall — this is where most of the increase in length actually occurs. The phase of maturation or differentiation follows, where cells attain their permanent form and function, develop thick or specialised walls, form vacuoles and become, for example, xylem vessels, root hairs or palisade cells. Growth in plants is confined to meristems: apical meristems at the tips of shoots and roots increase the length of the plant; lateral meristems, the vascular and cork cambia, increase its girth and are responsible for secondary thickening in woody plants; and intercalary meristems at the base of internodes and grass leaves allow a mown lawn to regrow. The whole of the plant body, in fact, is derived from two basic meristems — the procambium giving rise to the vascular tissues, and the cambium and cork cambium giving rise to the permanent tissues of the ground and dermal systems.

items: Growth is a permanent, irreversible increase measured as absolute or relative growth rate.

blocks.text: Plant hormones, or phytohormones, are chemical messengers produced in one part of the plant that act in another, often at very low concentrations, and they work by promoting or inhibiting growth rather than by driving it directly. Auxins, the first to be discovered, are indole compounds produced mainly in shoot apical meristems and young leaves and travel basipetally; they promote cell elongation, apical dominance, the bending of shoots towards light, root initiation on cuttings and the abscission of leaves, and they are also used commercially to root cuttings and to prevent premature fruit drop. Their effect on curvature was proved by Went’s agar block experiment: auxin collected in agar from coleoptile tips, and a block placed on one side of a decapitated coleoptile made it bend away from that side, showing that a diffusible chemical, not the tip itself, caused the curvature. Gibberellins promote stem elongation, break the dormancy of seeds such as barley, induce flowering in some species and enlarge fruit — the treatment of seedless grapes with gibberellic acid is the standard commercial example. Cytokinins promote cell division or cytokinesis, delay the ageing of leaves by delaying senescence, and work antagonistically with auxin in controlling shoot and root formation: a high auxin to cytokinin ratio promotes roots, a low ratio promotes shoots. Abscisic acid is the growth inhibitor: it maintains seed and bud dormancy, causes stomatal closure during water stress and therefore wilting, and offsets the effects of the growth promoters — it is often called the stress hormone. Ethylene is the only gaseous hormone, and it promotes the ripening of fruit, the abscission of leaves and flowers, and the triple response of a seedling; ripening fruit in a paper bag works because the trapped ethylene accelerates the process. Understanding these hormones also explains the synthetic herbicides: 2,4-D acts as an auxin at high concentration, causing unchecked growth and death in broad-leaved weeds while leaving grasses unaffected.

blocks.text: The mechanism by which auxin produces elongation illustrates how all these hormones work in principle. Auxin arrives at the cell on the side of elongation and binds to a receptor in the membrane or cytoplasm, and one widely accepted explanation of its effect is the acid growth hypothesis: auxin activates proton pumps in the plasma membrane, which secrete hydrogen ions into the wall and lower its pH. The acidic wall activates expansin enzymes that loosen the hydrogen bonds between cellulose microfibrils, so the wall becomes extensible; water then enters by osmosis and the turgid cell pushes the wall outwards, elongating. Auxin also switches on genes for new wall materials, so growth continues rather than merely stretching. The same logic — receptor, signal, gene expression or enzyme activation, cellular response — applies to gibberellins, which promote the production of hydrolytic enzymes in the barley endosperm during germination, and to abscisic acid, which closes stomata by triggering potassium and anion loss from guard cells so that they lose water and the pore shuts. Photoperiodism is the second mechanism topic. Flowering is triggered not by day length itself but by the length of the uninterrupted night, which the plant measures with the pigment phytochrome. Phytochrome exists in two interconvertible forms: Pr, which absorbs red light at about 660 nanometres, and Pfr, which absorbs far-red light at about 730 nanometres. Red light converts Pr to the active Pfr, far-red light converts Pfr back to Pr, and Pfr also reverts slowly to Pr during darkness. Short-day plants, which are more accurately long-night plants, flower when the night exceeds a critical length, because the long darkness lets Pfr fall below the threshold that would hold them vegetative — chrysanthemum and soybean are the standard examples. Long-day plants flower when the night is shorter than the critical length, since Pfr remains abundant — wheat, spinach and clover. Day-neutral plants such as tomato and rice flower regardless of photoperiod. A night interrupted by a flash of red light will not permit short-day flowering, but a subsequent flash of far-red light reverses the effect, which is the classic proof that phytochrome and not total light energy is the receptor.

blocks.text: The theory of hormones earns its place in the examination through the applications it explains, and four of them account for most of the questions asked. Vegetative propagation uses the fact that any cell carrying the full genome can regenerate a whole plant: cuttings are dipped in auxin powder to strike roots, the auxin promoting the cambium beneath the cut to divide and form root primordia, which is how roses, sugarcane and many ornamental plants are multiplied commercially. Tissue culture takes the principle further, growing an explant on a sterile medium whose auxin to cytokinin ratio decides whether it produces roots, shoots or an undifferentiated callus, so a single plant can be cloned into thousands of identical individuals in a few months — the method used for banana, orchid and gladiolus, where seed production would be too slow or absent. Fruit development is treated with growth regulators as well: seedless grapes are sprayed with gibellic acid to enlarge the berries, and untreated flowers that have not been pollinated can be induced to set fruit by applying auxin or a synthetic analogue to the stigma, which is how commercial tomato and cucumber growers produce fruit without bees. Weed control uses the same chemistry against itself: the synthetic auxin 2,4-D is applied at a concentration far above anything a plant makes naturally, and it causes the broad-leaved weed to grow uncontrollably, with distorted and unusable tissue, while the grass crops — whose narrower leaves and different growth pattern make them less sensitive — survive. The same reasoning explains the harvest treatments: ethylene from ripening fruit is used deliberately to ripen a crop uniformly by holding it in a sealed room with a controlled dose, and a chemical that blocks the action of ethylene can hold a crop back until it reaches the market. Every application follows from one principle — that a hormone acts at a specific concentration on a specific tissue — so a good answer always names the hormone, the concentration or balance, the tissue affected and the result.

Every application is a statement of hormone, dose, tissue and result.

questions.prompt: A flash of which light during the night prevents flowering in a short-day plant?
questions.explanation: Red light converts Pr to the active Pfr, which is as though the night had been cut short; a following far-red flash reverses it.

questions.prompt: The permanent and irreversible increase in size or dry mass of a plant is called __________.
questions.explanation: It is measured as absolute increase or as relative growth rate per unit of initial size.

questions.prompt: The pigment that exists in red-absorbing and far-red-absorbing forms and measures night length is __________.
questions.explanation: Pr absorbs red light and converts to Pfr, which absorbs far-red and reverts to Pr in darkness.

questions.prompt: Name the three phases of growth at the cellular level and give one feature of each.
questions.answer: The first is the meristematic phase, in which cells are small with thin walls, dense cytoplasm, large nuclei and no large vacuoles, and they divide actively to increase number. The second is the phase of elongation, in which the cells enlarge chiefly by taking up water into a developing vacuule so that the wall stretches and the organ lengthens. The third is the phase of maturation or differentiation, in which the cells assume their permanent shape and function, developing thick or specialised walls as xylem vessels, root hairs or palisade cells.
questions.explanation: All three phases named with one structural or functional feature each.

questions.answer: Auxin promotes cell elongation in shoots, which is why a coleoptile bends towards light when auxin accumulates on the shaded side where it travels. It causes apical dominance, in which the growing tip suppresses the outgrowth of lateral buds, so a plant grows tall rather than bushy unless the tip is removed. It also promotes the initiation of roots, which is why cuttings are treated with auxin powder to strike roots, and it delays the abscission of leaves and fruit.
questions.explanation: Any three of elongation, apical dominance, root initiation, phototropism and delayed abscission, each explained.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between absolute growth rate and relative growth rate.
questions.answer: Absolute growth rate is the increase in size or mass measured over a period — the total quantity by which the plant has grown, expressed for example in grams or centimetres per day. Relative growth rate is that increase expressed per unit of the initial quantity, so it measures how fast the plant is growing in proportion to its size. The distinction matters because two plants can show the same absolute increase while the smaller one is growing much faster relative to itself, and relative growth rate is therefore the fairer measure for comparing a seedling with a mature plant.
questions.explanation: Absolute as total increase, relative as increase per unit of initial size, with the reason the second allows comparison.

questions.prompt: Describe Went’s experiment on the phototropism of coleoptiles and state what it proved about the cause of curvature.
questions.answer: Went began by decapitating coleoptiles of oat seedlings, removing the tip that was known to be required for the bending response. He then placed the cut tips on blocks of agar for a period, during which the growth-promoting substance diffused out of the tips and into the agar. Agar that had not contacted a tip served as a control. He placed a block containing the substance on one side of a decapitated coleoptile, and on the opposite side a plain agar block as control, and then observed the growth of the coleoptile over several hours. The coleoptile bent away from the side carrying the treated block, because the cells on that side elongated faster than those on the control side. Since neither the tip nor any light stimulus was present during the curvature, the bending must have been caused by the diffusible chemical collected in the agar, which Went named auxin. The control block produced no curvature, confirming that agar alone had no effect. The experiment therefore proved three things: that the tip produces the growth-promoting substance, that it moves downwards, and that unequal distribution of that substance on the two sides of the organ is what produces asymmetric growth and so the curvature towards or away from light.
questions.explanation: Decapitation, agar collection, one-sided placement, the asymmetric growth observed, and the conclusions with the control noted.

questions.prompt: Explain how abscisic acid helps a plant survive a period of drought, and how it acts in opposition to the growth-promoting hormones.
questions.answer: During drought the plant faces two problems: water loss through the stomata and the continuation of growth that would demand water it does not have. Abscisic acid addresses both. As the soil dries and the leaves lose water, abscisic acid is synthesised and transported to the guard cells, where it triggers the efflux of potassium ions and accompanying anions; the solute concentration of the guard cells falls, water follows by osmosis, the cells become flaccid and the stomatal pore closes. This sharply reduces transpiration and conserves the water remaining in the tissues, at the cost of stopping carbon dioxide entry and so photosynthesis — a trade the plant accepts in order to survive. Abscisic acid also maintains the dormancy of buds and seeds, so the plant does not commit to new growth while conditions are unfavourable, and it promotes the hardening of tissues. In these actions it opposes the growth promoters: auxin and gibberellin drive elongation and cell expansion, cytokinin drives division, while abscisic acid holds those processes back, closes the very stomata that the promoters would keep open for growth, and enforces dormancy against the gibberellin-induced breaking of it. The balance between the promoters and abcisic acid therefore sets the plant’s response to the season, and it is this balance that a cultivar selected for drought tolerance has shifted in favour of abscisic acid.
questions.explanation: Both survival functions with the ion and water mechanism of stomatal closure, then the explicit opposition to auxin, gibberellin and cytokinin.

questions.prompt: A tissue culture experiment produces roots when the medium contains a high ratio of auxin to cytokinin, and shoots when the ratio is low. Explain the significance of this result.
questions.answer: The result shows that the two hormones do not act independently but as a ratio that the tissue reads to decide its developmental path, and that the fate of the undifferentiated cells is controlled by the balance of chemical signals rather than being fixed. At a high auxin to cytokinin ratio the cells are directed towards root formation: auxin at that balance activates the genes for root initiation and promotes the elongation needed for a root primordium to emerge, while the lower cytokinin does not drive shoot-forming division. When the ratio is reversed, with cytokinin predominant, cell division is promoted and the shoot apical programme is activated, so buds and shoots arise from the callus. An intermediate or balanced ratio tends to produce an undifferentiated callus rather than either organ. The practical significance is twofold. First, it makes micropropagation possible: a single explant can be multiplied into thousands of genetically identical plants by transferring it through media of different ratios, which is how commercial nurseries propagate bananas and orchids. Second, it demonstrates the principle that the response to a hormone depends on concentration and on the presence of the others, which is why the same substance can root a cutting at one concentration and act as a weedkiller at another.
questions.explanation: The ratio as the reading, what each balance produces with the mechanism, the intermediate callus, and the two practical consequences.
